claim: Chemoresistance is a major cause of treatment failure in many cancers.
source: Chemoresistance is a major cause of treatment failure in many cancers.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jazaeri et al., 2005 in the introduction section.

claim: Drug resistance is increased by tumor heterogeneity.
source: which is increased by tumor heterogeneity (Heppner and Miller, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Heppner and Miller, 1983.

claim: Microfluidic chips can manipulate and control fluids and particles at the micron level.
source: Microfluidic chips are highly useful for studying drug resistance because they can manipulate and control fluids and particles at the micron level (Yeo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yeo et al., 2011.

claim: A microfluidic platform with concentration gradients has been developed to induce drug resistance in triple negative breast cancer.
source: Recently, a microfluidic platform consisting of an array of connected microchambers with concentration gradients has been developed to induce drug resistance in various types of cancers, such as triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) (Han et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Han et al., 2019 and Wu et al., 2013.

claim: A microfluidic platform with concentration gradients has been developed to induce drug resistance in glioblastoma multiforme.
source: Recently, a microfluidic platform consisting of an array of connected microchambers with concentration gradients has been developed to induce drug resistance in various types of cancers, such as triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) (Han et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2013), glioblastoma multiforme (GBM; Han et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2016.

claim: A microfluidic platform with concentration gradients has been developed to induce drug resistance in prostate cancer.
source: Recently, a microfluidic platform consisting of an array of connected microchambers with concentration gradients has been developed to induce drug resistance in various types of cancers, such as triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) (Han et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2013), glioblastoma multiforme (GBM; Han et al., 2016), and prostate cancer (Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2020.

claim: The CDRA chip can generate gradients of DOX and medium to induce DOX-resistant cells from MDA-MB-231 TNBC cells within 11 days.
source: In this study, we utilized the Cancer Drug Resistance Accelerator (CDRA) chip (Han et al., 2016) to generate gradients of DOX and medium to induce DOX-resistant (DOXR) cells from MDA-MB-231 TNBC cells within 11 days.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the manuscript and citation to Han et al., 2016.

claim: A subpopulation of very large cells (L-DOXR cells) emerged within the DOXR cell population in the CDRA chip on day 11.
source: Interestingly, a subpopulation of very large cells, referred to as L-DOXR cells, emerged within the DOXR cell population in the CDRA chip on day 11.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: L-DOXR cells were isolated using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) and maintained their survival off the chip.
source: These L-DOXR cells were isolated using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) and maintained their survival off the chip.
evidence: Supported by experimental methods described in the manuscript.

claim: The chemoresistance of L-DOXR cells is attributed to failed epigenetic control of nuclear protein-1 (NUPR1)/histone deacetylase 11 (HDAC11) axis.
source: Our results demonstrate that the chemoresistance of L-DOXR cells is attributed to failed epigenetic control of nuclear protein-1 (NUPR1)/histone deacetylase 11 (HDAC11) axis, which can be alleviated through NUPR1 inhibition (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 1 showing the overall study design and findings.

claim: NUPR1 is involved in multiple aspects of cancer, including DNA repair, transcription regulation, and the cell cycle.
source: NUPR1, which is also known as Com-1 or p8, is involved in multiple aspects of cancer, including DNA repair, transcription regulation, and the cell cycle, and its expression responds to stress signals induced by genotoxic signals and agents (Martin et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martin et al., 2021.

claim: NUPR1 influences cancer cell resistance.
source: NUPR1 influences cancer cell resistance (Hamidi et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hamidi et al., 2012.

claim: NUPR1 promotes the proliferation of cancer cells bypassing the G0/G1 check point.
source: NUPR1 influences cancer cell resistance (Hamidi et al., 2012) and promotes the proliferation of cancer cells bypassing the G0/G1 check point (Brannon-Peppas et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brannon-Peppas et al., 2007.

claim: In breast cancer cells, NUPR1 upregulates p21 transcription, allowing breast cancer cells to progress through the cell cycle.
source: In breast cancer cells, NUPR1 upregulates p21 transcription, allowing breast cancer cells to progress through the cell cycle, and it confers resistance to chemotherapeutic agents such as taxol and DOX (Clark et al., 2008; Vincent et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clark et al., 2008 and Vincent et al., 2012.

claim: NUPR1 confers resistance to chemotherapeutic agents such as taxol and DOX in breast cancer cells.
source: In breast cancer cells, NUPR1 upregulates p21 transcription, allowing breast cancer cells to progress through the cell cycle, and it confers resistance to chemotherapeutic agents such as taxol and DOX (Clark et al., 2008; Vincent et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clark et al., 2008 and Vincent et al., 2012.

claim: Increased expression of NUPR1 has been associated with poor patient outcomes in certain types of cancers.
source: Increased expression of NUPR1 has previously been associated with poor patient outcomes in certain types of cancers (Jung et al., 2012; Mu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jung et al., 2012 and Mu et al., 2018.

claim: HDAC11 is the most recently discovered member of the HDAC family and the only member of class IV.
source: Histone deacetylase 11 (HDAC11) is the most recently discovered member of the HDAC family and the only member of class IV.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about HDAC classification.

claim: HDAC11 displays different expression levels and biological functions in different human organs and systems.
source: It displays different expression levels and biological functions in different human organs and systems.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about HDAC11.

claim: HDAC11 is overexpressed in hepatocellular cancer.
source: Its overexpression in various cancers, including hepatocellular, ovarian, myeloma, lymphoma, and breast cancers (Gong et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2020; Yue et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: HDAC11 is overexpressed in ovarian cancer.
source: Its overexpression in various cancers, including hepatocellular, ovarian, myeloma, lymphoma, and breast cancers (Gong et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2020; Yue et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: HDAC11 is overexpressed in myeloma.
source: Its overexpression in various cancers, including hepatocellular, ovarian, myeloma, lymphoma, and breast cancers (Gong et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2020; Yue et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: HDAC11 is overexpressed in lymphoma.
source: Its overexpression in various cancers, including hepatocellular, ovarian, myeloma, lymphoma, and breast cancers (Gong et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2020; Yue et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: HDAC11 is overexpressed in breast cancers.
source: Its overexpression in various cancers, including hepatocellular, ovarian, myeloma, lymphoma, and breast cancers (Gong et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2020; Yue et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: HDAC11 expression is negatively correlated with high-risk uveal melanomas.
source: However, HDAC11 expression is negatively correlated with high-risk uveal melanomas and gliomas (Dali-Youcef et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dali-Youcef et al., 2015.

claim: HDAC11 expression is negatively correlated with gliomas.
source: However, HDAC11 expression is negatively correlated with high-risk uveal melanomas and gliomas (Dali-Youcef et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dali-Youcef et al., 2015.

claim: HDAC11 knockout mice demonstrate increased tumor growth.
source: and HDAC11 knockout mice demonstrate increased tumor growth (Sahakian et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sahakian et al., 2015.

claim: Approximately 30 wild type MDA-MB-231 cells per microchamber were seeded through the cell seeding hole in the CDRA chip.
source: Approximately 30 wild type MDA-MB-231 cells per microchamber were seeded through the cell seeding hole in the CDRA chip (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental description and Figure 2A-C.

claim: Cells were perfused with gradients of medium and DOX (1.5 μM) the day after seeding.
source: The day after seeding, the cells were perfused with gradients of medium and DOX (1.5 μM; Figure 2A, B and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental description and Figure 2.

claim: Cells exposed to a high concentration of DOX were killed within 5 days.
source: Cells exposed to a high concentration of DOX (high-DOX region) were killed within 5 days, whereas those exposed to an intermediate concentration of DOX (mid-DOX region) began to die on day 5 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cells exposed to an intermediate concentration of DOX began to die on day 5.
source: Cells exposed to a high concentration of DOX (high-DOX region) were killed within 5 days, whereas those exposed to an intermediate concentration of DOX (mid-DOX region) began to die on day 5 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2E.

claim: DOXR cells appeared and proliferated in the mid-DOX region on day 8.
source: On day 8, DOXR cells appeared and proliferated in the mid-DOX region.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.

claim: A population of phenotypically large cells (L-DOXR) appeared in the mid-DOX region on day 11.
source: On day 11, a population of phenotypically large cells (L-DOXR) appeared in the mid-DOX region (Figure 2D and E)
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: L-DOXR cells emerge from stressful but tolerable conditions on the chip in areas where an intermediate concentration of DOX is perfused.
source: suggesting that they emerge from stressful but tolerable conditions on the chip in areas where an intermediate concentration of DOX is perfused.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: The proportions of polyploidy (cells greater than 4N+) in the WT cells, DOXR cells, and L-DOXR cells were 2, 15, and 40%, respectively.
source: The FACS cell cycle analysis showed that the proportions of polyploidy (cells greater than 4N+) in the WT cells, DOXR cells, and L-DOXR cells were 2, 15, and 40%, respectively (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: L-DOXR cells showed lower susceptibility to DOX than the WT and DOXR cells.
source: The L-DOXR cells showed lower susceptibility to DOX than the WT and DOXR cells (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I-K.

claim: The CDRA chip can rapidly induce the development of DOXR cells as well as a distinct population of L-DOXR cells.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the CDRA chip can rapidly induce the development of DOXR cells as well as a distinct population of L-DOXR cells.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental results presented.

claim: L-DOXR cells exhibited significantly higher rates of proliferation compared to WT cells.
source: Our results showed that L-DOXR cells exhibited significantly higher rates of proliferation and a greater proportion of Ki67-positive cells compared to WT cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: L-DOXR cells exhibited a greater proportion of Ki67-positive cells compared to WT cells.
source: Our results showed that L-DOXR cells exhibited significantly higher rates of proliferation and a greater proportion of Ki67-positive cells compared to WT cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: L-DOXR cells migrated faster than WT cells in an in vitro wound-healing assay.
source: An in vitro wound-healing assay showed L-DOXR cells migrated faster than WT cells, suggesting that the development of L-DOXR cells could increase the migration capacity of a TNBC cancer cell population (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The development of L-DOXR cells could increase the migration capacity of a TNBC cancer cell population.
source: An in vitro wound-healing assay showed L-DOXR cells migrated faster than WT cells, suggesting that the development of L-DOXR cells could increase the migration capacity of a TNBC cancer cell population (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on inference from wound-healing assay results.

claim: Mice injected with L-DOXR cells showed much larger tumors compared to mice injected with WT cells, irrespective of DOX treatment.
source: Irrespective of DOX treatment, the mice injected with L-DOXR cells showed much larger tumors compared to the mice injected with WT cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The tumor volume of L-DOXR cells treated with DOX and vehicle did not differ significantly.
source: The tumor volume of L-DOXR cells treated with DOX and vehicle did not differ significantly (p>0.05), but the tumor volume of WT cells treated with DOX was significantly smaller than that of WT cells treated with vehicle (p<0.001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of tumor volume data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The tumor volume of WT cells treated with DOX was significantly smaller than that of WT cells treated with vehicle.
source: The tumor volume of L-DOXR cells treated with DOX and vehicle did not differ significantly (p>0.05), but the tumor volume of WT cells treated with DOX was significantly smaller than that of WT cells treated with vehicle (p<0.001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of tumor volume data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: L-DOXR tumors did not exhibit a reduction in cell density or proliferation upon DOX treatment, in contrast to WT cells.
source: Our findings are consistent with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (Figure 3G, top) and immunohistochemical staining for proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) (Figure 3G, bottom) in the tumor tissues, which indicate that L-DOXR tumors did not exhibit a reduction in cell density or proliferation upon DOX treatment, in contrast to WT cells.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: L-DOXR cells in TNBC developed in the CDRA chip significantly enhanced carcinogenesis.
source: Therefore, the L-DOXR cells in TNBC developed in the CDRA chip significantly enhanced carcinogenesis, and tumors initiated with L-DOXR cells were no longer sensitive to DOX.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental results presented.

claim: Tumors initiated with L-DOXR cells were no longer sensitive to DOX.
source: Therefore, the L-DOXR cells in TNBC developed in the CDRA chip significantly enhanced carcinogenesis, and tumors initiated with L-DOXR cells were no longer sensitive to DOX.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental results presented.

claim: L-DOXR cells exhibit increased genomic content (4N+) as compared to WT cells.
source: L-DOXR cells exhibit increased genomic content (4N+) as compared to WT cells.
evidence: Supported by FACS cell cycle analysis data.

claim: The presence of cells with increased nuclear size and increased genomic content has been demonstrated to be associated with poor clinical outcomes in several types of cancers.
source: The presence of cells with increased nuclear size and increased genomic content has been demonstrated to be associated with poor clinical outcomes in several types of cancers (Alharbi et al., 2018; Amend et al., 2019; Fei et al., 2015; Imai et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2018; Lv et al., 2014; Mukherjee et al., 2022; O'Connor et al., 2002; Saini et al., 2022; Trabzonlu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cells with increased nuclear size/genomic content were found only in TNBC patient tissues but not in normal breast tissue.
source: A tissue microarray (TMA; n=130) found cells with increased nuclear size/genomic content only in TNBC patient tissues but not in normal breast tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by tissue microarray analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The number of cells with large nuclei in each tissue correlated with tumor grade.
source: In addition, the number of cells with large nuclei in each tissue correlated with tumor grade (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by tissue microarray analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The presence of cells with increased genomic content in TNBC may indicate the presence of cells that are resistant to therapy.
source: Therefore, the presence of cells with increased genomic content in TNBC may indicate the presence of cells that are resistant to therapy.
evidence: Based on inference from the correlation between large cells and tumor grade.

claim: Among the genes whose expression was significantly altered (fold change cut-off=2), 1212 were upregulated and 1,602 were downregulated in the L-DOXR cells.
source: Among the genes whose expression was significantly altered (fold change cut-off=2), 1212 were upregulated and 1,602 were downregulated in the L-DOXR cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NUPR1 was top-ranked in the Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of genes upregulated in L-DOXR cells.
source: An Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) revealed that NUPR1, whose upregulation is associated with malignancy of cancer and the chemoresistance network (Wang et al., 2021), was top-ranked
evidence: Supported by IPA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Antioxidant signaling was the most enriched pathway in L-DOXR cells.
source: and antioxidant signaling was the most enriched pathway along with other cancer-promoting signaling such as tumor necrosis factor receptor 2, mitogen-activated protein kinase, and phospholipase signaling (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: NUPR1 is responsible for 4.4% (53/1212) of the genes actively transcribed in the L-DOXR cells.
source: Notably, the upstream regulator analysis in IPA revealed that NUPR1 is a high-rank regulator and is responsible for 4.4% (53/1212) of the genes actively transcribed in the L-DOXR cells (cut-off=1.5, p<0.05) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by upstream regulator analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The overall survival rate was significantly lower in chemotherapy-treated TNBC patients with high NUPR1 mRNA expression than in patients whose NUPR1 mRNA expression was low.
source: The overall survival rate was significantly lower in patients with high NUPR1 mRNA expression than in patients whose NUPR1 mRNA expression was low (high, n=34; low, n=32; p=0.037; Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Chemotherapy-treated breast cancer patients with significantly lower survival rates expressed higher level of NUPR1 in datasets GSE12093 and GSE16391.
source: Similarly, in other datasets GSE12093 (Zhang et al., 2009; Figure 4E) and GSE16391 (Desmedt et al., 2009), chemotherapy-treated breast cancer patients with significantly lower survival rates expressed higher level of NUPR1 (p=0.027 and 0.0003, respectively; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by survival analysis of patient datasets shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: High NUPR1 expression is associated with poor clinical outcomes among TNBC patients.
source: suggesting that high NUPR1 expression is associated with poor clinical outcomes among TNBC patients.
evidence: Based on inference from survival analysis data.

claim: Increased expression of NUPR1 was observed in both the L-DOXR cells and L-DOXR cell-derived xenografts.
source: Consistent with the RNA-seq analysis of L-DOXR cells, increased expression of NUPR1 in both the L-DOXR cells and L-DOXR cell-derived xenografts were observed in reverse transcriptase-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR; Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: mRNA level of NUPR1 was barely detectable in the WT cells and WT cell-derived tumor tissues.
source: However, in contrast to L-DOXR cells, mRNA level of NUPR1 was barely detectable in the WT cells and WT cell-derived tumor tissues.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data.

claim: DOXR cells exhibited a marked increase in NUPR1 expression compared to the WT cells, but this expression was substantially less than that observed in L-DOXR cells.
source: While DOXR cells exhibited a marked increase in NUPR1 expression compared to the WT cells, this expression was substantially less than that observed in L-DOXR cells, as detailed in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Transactivation activity of the NUPR1 promoter was highly elevated in L-DOXR cells but not in WT cells.
source: Furthermore, transactivation activity of the NUPR1 promoter was highly elevated in L-DOXR cells but not in WT cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: NUPR1 expression is highly enhanced in L-DOXR cells.
source: These results indicate that NUPR1 expression is highly enhanced in L-DOXR cells.
evidence: Based on inference from RT-qPCR and luciferase assay results.

claim: Silencing NUPR1 expression abolished the cell viability of DOX-treated L-DOXR cells.
source: Silencing NUPR1 expression abolished the cell viability of DOX-treated L-DOXR cells, but it did not decrease the cell viability of vehicle-treated L-DOXR cells, suggesting that NUPR1 depletion could eliminate DOX resistance in L-DOXR cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NUPR1 depletion did not decrease the cell viability of vehicle-treated L-DOXR cells.
source: Silencing NUPR1 expression abolished the cell viability of DOX-treated L-DOXR cells, but it did not decrease the cell viability of vehicle-treated L-DOXR cells, suggesting that NUPR1 depletion could eliminate DOX resistance in L-DOXR cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NUPR1 depletion could eliminate DOX resistance in L-DOXR cells.
source: Silencing NUPR1 expression abolished the cell viability of DOX-treated L-DOXR cells, but it did not decrease the cell viability of vehicle-treated L-DOXR cells, suggesting that NUPR1 depletion could eliminate DOX resistance in L-DOXR cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Based on inference from cell viability assay results.

claim: NUPR1 depletion did not affect the chemosensitivity of WT cells regardless of DOX-treatment.
source: Regardless of DOX-treatment, NUPR1 depletion did not affect the chemosensitivity of WT cells.
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data.

claim: Overexpression of NUPR1 in the WT cells attenuates DOX-induced cytotoxicity.
source: In addition, we showed that overexpression of NUPR1 in the WT cells attenuates DOX-induced cytotoxicity (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: NUPR1 upregulation may be a major driver of chemoresistance in L-DOXR cells.
source: These results suggest that NUPR1 upregulation may be a major driver of chemoresistance in L-DOXR cells.
evidence: Based on inference from NUPR1 knockdown and overexpression experiments.

claim: ZZW-115 is a NUPR1 inhibitor that alters its nuclear localization.
source: To define the potential role of NUPR1 in mediating chemoresistance in TNBC, we treated WT cells and L-DOXR cells with ZZW-115, a NUPR1 inhibitor that alters its nuclear localization (Lan et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lan et al., 2020.

claim: ZZW-115 treatment led to re-sensitization of L-DOXR cells to DOX in a dose-dependent manner.
source: ZZW-115 treatment led to re-sensitization of L-DOXR cells to DOX in a dose-dependent manner, whereas the WT cells barely responded to ZZW-115 (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: WT cells barely responded to ZZW-115.
source: ZZW-115 treatment led to re-sensitization of L-DOXR cells to DOX in a dose-dependent manner, whereas the WT cells barely responded to ZZW-115 (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Delocalization of NUPR1 and increased cell death caused by ZZW-115 were confirmed by immunocytochemistry.
source: Delocalization of NUPR1 and increased cell death caused by ZZW-115 were confirmed by immunocytochemistry (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and active CASPASE-3 and poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) cleavage (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Increased cell death caused by ZZW-115 was confirmed by active CASPASE-3 and PARP cleavage.
source: Delocalization of NUPR1 and increased cell death caused by ZZW-115 were confirmed by immunocytochemistry (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and active CASPASE-3 and poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) cleavage (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The addition of ZZW-115 to DOX in the xenograft models resulted in a reduction of tumor volume compared to DOX-only-treated tumors.
source: The addition of ZZW-115 to DOX in the xenograft models resulted in a reduction of tumor volume compared to DOX-only-treated tumors (–469.5 ± 25.20 mm3 [2.5 mg/kg] and –627.2±15.36 [5.0 mg/kg]) (Figure 4M-O; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: Supported by in vivo tumor volume measurements shown in Figure 4M-O and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The addition of ZZW-115 to DOX in the xenograft models induced significant cell death.
source: and induced significant cell death (Figure 4P).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 4P.

claim: NUPR1 inhibition can overcome chemoresistance in highly aggressive L-DOXR cell-induced tumors in xenograft model mice.
source: These findings suggest that NUPR1 inhibition can overcome chemoresistance in highly aggressive L-DOXR cell-induced tumors in xenograft model mice.
evidence: Based on inference from in vivo xenograft experiments.

claim: No remarkable changes in promoter methylation were found between WT cells and L-DOXR cells.
source: However, we did not find any remarkable changes in promoter methylation between WT cells L-DOXR cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by DNA methylation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ChIP-qPCR using the histone H3 at lysine 27 (H3K27)-acetylation antibody revealed H3K27 acetylation in L-DOXR cells, specifically in promoter region 3.
source: Intriguingly, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-qPCR using the histone H3 at lysine 27 (H3K27)-acetylation antibody revealed H3K27 acetylation in L-DOXR cells, specifically in promoter region 3 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: RNA-seq analysis showed almost no detectable mRNA expression of HDAC11 in L-DOXR cells.
source: An RNA-seq analysis of HATs and HDACs in WT cells and L-DOXR cells showed almost no detectable mRNA expression of HDAC11 in L-DOXR cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RT-qPCR confirmed almost no detectable mRNA expression of HDAC11 in L-DOXR cells.
source: which we confirmed by RT-qPCR (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: HDAC11 expression was dramatically reduced in tumors from L-DOXR cell-derived xenografts compared with tumors derived from WT cells.
source: HDAC11 expression was also dramatically reduced in tumors from L-DOXR cell-derived xenografts compared with tumors derived from WT cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The protein expression of NUPR1 and HDAC11 was inversely correlated in L-DOXR cells and WT cells.
source: In addition, the protein expression of NUPR1 and HDAC11 was inversely correlated in L-DOXR cells and WT cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D)
evidence: Supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Low levels of HDAC11 in L-DOXR cells might contribute to the upregulation of NUPR1 through enriched acetylation in its promoter region.
source: suggesting that low levels of HDAC11 in L-DOXR cells might contribute to the upregulation of NUPR1 through enriched acetylation in its promoter region.
evidence: Based on inference from the inverse correlation between HDAC11 and NUPR1 expression and the acetylation data.

claim: Forced expression of HDAC11 elicited a dramatic reduction in H3K27 acetylation in the L-DOXR cells promoter region.
source: Indeed, forced expression of HDAC11 elicited a dramatic reduction in H3K27 acetylation in the L-DOXR cells promoter region (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Forced expression of HDAC11 reduced the mRNA expression of NUPR1 in a dose-dependent manner in L-DOXR cells but not in the parental WT cells.
source: which reduced the mRNA expression of NUPR1 in a dose-dependent manner not seen in the parental WT cells (Figure 5E)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Forced expression of HDAC11 greatly impaired the promoter activity in the L-DOXR cells.
source: and also greatly impaired the promoter activity in the L-DOXR cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: HDAC11 inhibitor treatment in WT cells augmented the expression of NUPR1.
source: Moreover, HDAC11 inhibitor treatment in WT cells augmented the expression of NUPR1, presumably, reflecting the reverting of promoter acetylation (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: HDAC11 mediates NUPR1 promoter deacetylation.
source: These data clearly demonstrate that HDAC11 mediates NUPR1 promoter deacetylation
evidence: Based on inference from HDAC11 overexpression and inhibition experiments.

claim: The suppressed expression of HDAC11 in L-DOXR cells allows NUPR1 to escape deacetylation and thereby causes its aberrant high expression.
source: underscoring that the suppressed expression of HDAC11 in L-DOXR cells allows NUPR1 to escape deacetylation and thereby causes its aberrant high expression.
evidence: Based on inference from the mechanistic studies of HDAC11 and NUPR1.

claim: As tumor grade increased, NUPR1 expression increased in TNBC patient tissues.
source: In a tissue microarray (TMA) of TNBC patient tissues (n=130), we verified that, as tumor grade increased, NUPR1 expression increased and HDAC11 expression decreased (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by tissue microarray analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: As tumor grade increased, HDAC11 expression decreased in TNBC patient tissues.
source: In a tissue microarray (TMA) of TNBC patient tissues (n=130), we verified that, as tumor grade increased, NUPR1 expression increased and HDAC11 expression decreased (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by tissue microarray analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Patients with low HDAC11 expression had significantly shorter survival times than patients with high HDAC11 expression after chemotherapy.
source: In addition, a KM plot analysis of breast cancer patients (n=500, HER negative) from GSE25066 (Hatzis et al., 2011) showed that patients with low HDAC11 expression had significantly shorter survival times than patients with high HDAC11 expression after chemotherapy (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
